data.name: Rubber Ball VR
data.detailed_description:
Rubber Ball VR is a virtual reality game where you can satisfy your need to throw cool trickshots, all without the mess of having to go and fetch your ball again.

Features

  • Chose between 3 different ball types to reach the goal
  • Complete 50 maps
  • Use trampolines, avoid lava, shoot cannons and more!
  • Beat your own high score in number of balls you have to spawn on each map

This game will continue to be updated with bug fixes, and eventually new maps if the interest for it is enough. This is our first game and we are therefore really interested in your feedback so please visit our website to give feedback!

reviews.review:
Rubber Ball VR is a straightforward virtual reality physics game that turns the simple act of throwing a ball into a collection of compact challenges. Developed and published by Viraug, the game comes from an earlier period of consumer VR when developers were experimenting with motion controls and finding activities that felt natural with tracked controllers. Its premise is easy to understand: pick up a ball, aim for the objective, and figure out how to overcome whatever obstacles stand between you and the target. It does not attempt to surround this concept with an elaborate story or complicated progression system, instead relying almost entirely on physics and player experimentation.

The game contains 50 maps built around increasingly varied throwing challenges. A direct shot is not always possible, so players must consider trajectories, rebounds, environmental objects, and the behavior of the available balls. Trampolines can launch balls into otherwise inaccessible areas, cannons provide alternative methods of sending them toward their destination, and dangerous surfaces such as lava force players to think more carefully about positioning. These mechanics give the experience a puzzle-like quality because accurate throwing alone will not necessarily solve every stage. Finding the correct route can be just as important as executing the final throw.

Three different types of balls provide additional opportunities for experimentation. Learning how each behaves within the physics system becomes part of solving the stages, while the ability to quickly spawn another ball keeps failed attempts from becoming frustrating. There is no need to physically chase a missed ball around the environment, so players can immediately correct their angle and try again. This creates a quick trial-and-error loop that works particularly well in virtual reality, where manually performing each throw makes even simple interactions feel more physical than they would with conventional controls.

Efficiency also provides an incentive to improve. Completing a stage is only the basic objective, while finishing it after spawning fewer balls offers an additional challenge. A player might initially waste numerous attempts discovering the correct solution before eventually returning and completing the same map much more efficiently. This gives the otherwise limited collection of stages some replay value. Players who enjoy perfecting trick shots can potentially spend additional time reducing unnecessary throws, although there is not enough mechanical depth to support extensive long-term progression.

Presentation is where the game's modest origins become most apparent. Environments and objects are functional rather than visually impressive, with relatively simple models and limited texturing. The minimalist appearance does at least keep the action readable, since important objects are generally easy to identify, but anyone expecting the polish of a modern VR production will find it noticeably dated. The lightweight presentation reflects the project's experimental character more than a carefully refined artistic direction.

A more significant concern is its Early Access status. The original development plans included additional puzzle maps, improved models and textures, bug fixes, and other refinements. However, development did not progress into the more complete experience originally envisioned, leaving the existing version feeling like a functional prototype that was expanded enough to provide a reasonable selection of levels but never received a comprehensive final polishing pass. This context is important because players should approach the game for what it currently provides rather than expecting substantial future improvements.

As a free VR title, however, those limitations are easier to forgive. There is something pleasantly uncomplicated about entering a stage and immediately understanding the objective without tutorials filled with systems and menus. Throwing, bouncing, launching, and redirecting balls provide simple physical entertainment, and the short challenge format makes the game suitable for brief sessions. The small installation footprint is another advantage for players who simply want an additional experimental VR title in their library without committing much storage space.

Steam Deck compatibility is effectively unsuitable for normal handheld play. Rubber Ball VR is designed as a VR-only experience that depends on SteamVR and tracked motion controllers, hardware that the Steam Deck by itself does not provide. Even if technical experimentation could potentially make portions of the software launch through unconventional configurations, the Deck's integrated controls and display cannot reproduce the intended VR interaction. It should therefore not be considered a practical Steam Deck game.

Rubber Ball VR is ultimately best understood as a modest VR physics playground rather than a fully realized puzzle or sports game. Its 50 maps, multiple ball types, environmental obstacles, cannons, trampolines, and efficiency-based challenges provide enough variety to demonstrate that the central throwing mechanic has potential. The lack of refinement and unfinished Early Access development prevent it from becoming something more substantial, but the basic physics interactions can still be entertaining for players with compatible VR equipment. As a small free experiment from the earlier days of SteamVR, it offers a simple reminder that sometimes an enjoyable VR mechanic can begin with something as basic as throwing a rubber ball at a target.

Rating: 6/10
